items.question: How do you assess AI’s progress toward human intelligence in light of achievements such as GPT-4’s exam performance and programs that beat humans at chess and Go?
items.object: AI progress toward human intelligence
items.answer: To me, this is something which has been known at least in a segment of the AI community for a while as Moravec’s paradox. We can tie it to the history of intelligence as a whole. If we think of intelligence as the biological construct which emerged through evolution, going back like 550 million years ago, when we have the first animals that can move, and then they can see—and seeing is important to moving, because that’s how you get to know where to go to find food and so on—and then on to, let’s say, the last seven million years, when you have the evolution of hominids from other primates. There is this very nice evolutionary data from fossils, which is that the evolution of the brain followed the evolution of the hand as an opposable hand with a thumb, which is opposable. This comes after we became bipedal. We started to walk on two feet, so the hand was free to build tools and manipulate objects, and then the opposable thumb helped us. Toolmaking led to humans getting an advantage over other species, even though they are, as such, quite small and frail compared to many other animals. And then, of course, we have the emergence of language. By a rough calculation, it’s something like this: if you think of all of evolutionary history as 24 hours, then language is the last two or three minutes. Language, symbolic thinking, and many of the things that we associate with sophisticated reasoning. So, in a sense, it’s remarkable that GPT-4 can do at the 90 level in the law exam, or in various tests of various sorts. I mean, this is incredible, and from the perspective of the general public, this is a sign of great intelligence. I would like to connect this back to achievements of AI even 20 years ago, when we had the first programs that could beat humans at chess, like, I think, in the late 90s. Then, of course, we had the DeepMind work, where they showed that their programs could beat humans at Go. These are remarkable, and to the general public, performance at these games is the ultimate achievement in intelligence. It is remarkable. I’m not trying to downgrade that accomplishment, but to me all the stuff which precedes that kind of level of accomplishment is equally important. This includes basic sensorimotor competence: the ability to see, move, manipulate objects, plan, and so on. That’s where I am, and I feel that we will not have conquered intelligence until we have conquered all those aspects of intelligence as well.

items.question: How do you understand the evidence that the development of the human hand preceded the development of the brain?
items.object: The evolutionary relationship between the human hand and intelligence
items.answer: The fossil data is about the size of the skull, and there’s data on the hand. What we have are fossils corresponding to the structure of the hand, and in the fossil record we can get an idea of that. We can get a sense of the volume of the cavity of the head in which the brain is. We can use those to connect up. The soft tissue inside the brain is never preserved in these fossils, so we can’t answer some very specific questions. There was this debate, which actually goes back to Greek philosophy: is it because we are intelligent that we can manipulate objects well, or is it because we manipulate objects well that we became intelligent? There’s a quote I like from a Greek philosopher called Anaxagoras, which is that it is because of his hand that man is the most intelligent of other animals. That could be a debate, right? But from the fossil evidence, we actually know the sequencing, which came first, and it appears to follow the order where the development of the hand led to the development of the brain in some ways, because that bigger brain could exploit that.

items.question: How do you think grounding language in physical experience matters for the development of intelligence?
items.object: Sensorimotor grounding in language learning and the development of intelligence
items.answer: To some extent, it’s an experimental question, which over time our field will answer. But let me tell you my bias on this. If we take developmental life, the life of a child, the early stage of a child is very much a sensorimotor stage. The child is playing around with objects, learning to crawl, then learning to walk, and of course the child is also being provided linguistic input from the parents or other caregivers. But that linguistic input is very grounded, right? The mother may say, “Give me the ball,” and there is a very clear object in front which the child knows is the ball, and then the word “give” has a very clear meaning, a referent in terms of an action, and so forth. The early words that a child acquires are very grounded in sensorimotor experience. They evoke the word “ball,” evoke a visual impression. It also evokes a motor impression: I see a ball, I feel like throwing it. This is what Gibson called affordances. A chair, as a visual image, sort of tells me how to sit down. There’s a motor action. The early words in a child’s vocabulary are of this nature. Then the child acquires these words and verbs, subject-verb-object triplets, and so forth. This is the beginning of language, and then it gets more elaborate. Later on, the child goes to school and starts reading books. In the books there are all these beautiful sentences and texts, and there are words like justice, peace, and fairness. Many of those words acquire their meaning in context. I don’t necessarily have an immediate visual picture of what fairness is, but I do have that concept, that it is related to other concepts. The kind of learning we are doing at that stage: we don’t go around looking up the meanings of individual words in dictionaries. We read and acquire meaning by context. This is pretty close to what’s happening inside these language models like GPT-3 and GPT-4. There’s a word which is deleted; you try to predict that from the context. I think that process is fairly close to the process of how we acquire knowledge when we read books as humans throughout our schooling and throughout life. But there was that earlier stage, right, which was very directly grounded. For a grown adult, maybe 80% of their vocabulary was acquired through these words whose meaning was captured in context, but I’m arguing that that 20% came first and is also very important. What we need to do, for the full development of intelligence, is sort of capture that. Language models which are not grounded will miss out on this aspect. I don’t view this as a fundamental failing, because clearly there are now models that people are developing which are vision and language.

items.question: Why do you favor building physical intelligence before language in AI?
items.object: Building physical intelligence before language in AI
items.answer: I don’t have hard scientific evidence on this, so this is a question of one’s belief and judgment call. I’m of the grounding-first school, but I’m willing to be proved wrong. I think of it this way. Let me give sort of slightly speculative evidence in favor of my beliefs: many of the words in language are evolved by metaphors. We talk about climbing the ladder of success. We use the spatial-temporal world, the world of movement, movement of objects, movement of agents, agents causing things, causing something to happen to an object, and so on. That is very much something on which the metaphors are very much central to language. George Lakoff, a linguist at Berkeley, has written books on this topic, emphasizing the importance of metaphor for language. He was doing this essentially to counter Chomsky, who had a much more formalistic grammar-type approach, that language in usage is built up with this laddering of a metaphor. In that sense, that would essentially argue to me that it might be easier to build language that way. Of course, we also know that we can build skills without language, because certainly crows have intelligent behavior, and gorillas and chimpanzees have intelligent behavior. The building of motor skills—the ability to open a door handle, insert a peg into a hole, thread a needle—doesn’t fundamentally require language. The development of that, as a purely scientific matter, should proceed without needing the layering of language. But time will tell. I’m betting my scientific career on the physical intelligence first, followed by language.

items.question: How do you understand the difficulty of the sensorimotor skills children acquire in their early years?
items.object: Children’s acquisition of sensorimotor skills
items.answer: These are essentially challenges of sensorimotor coordination, if you will: the ability of a child to manipulate objects, pick up objects, recognize objects, throw balls, assemble Lego pieces together. All of these are not easy, and we think of them as easy because as adults we can do them easily. But if you observe your child at the age of two and three, you will find that they have to do an enormous amount of practice. There is data on this because our colleagues in psychology are studying how children acquire these abilities. For example, Karen Adolph at NYU has studied how children learn to walk. She did it in a way where she was trying to be as ecologically valid as possible, observing children in a more natural setting. It turns out that they just fall a lot. That’s part of the process of learning to walk. They fall a lot; it doesn’t hurt them so much because their bodies are soft, there’s a lot of fat, they’re relatively short, so the center of gravity—the fall is not too big. They somehow just get up and start trying again. She shared these numbers on how many falls it is, and it’s quite a lot. Similarly, with attempts to manipulate objects, the children seem to be just trying to do various activities which are of interest to them and acquire these skills.

items.question: Why do you see age five as a meaningful milestone in children’s acquisition of foundational capabilities?
items.object: Age five as a milestone in children’s development
items.answer: I almost think of the age five you mentioned—age five is actually set by this, because you can’t send a child to school to start to learn to write if they cannot hold a pencil and manipulate it. Fine motor control has to come to a certain threshold level of capability before you subject a child to the discipline of learning to write. So that five threshold that you pick is actually related to the acquisition of certain expertise. Of course, it’s not just sensorimotor; there is also social expertise. Children acquire the ability to build and develop models of other agents, their caregivers, other children. They learn to figure out that they have goals. They learn how to work with mutual attention. There are a lot of sophisticated capabilities that have been acquired by age five.

items.question: How do you think about sensorimotor skill acquisition as a research agenda for robotics?
items.object: Sensorimotor skill acquisition and the composition of complex skills
items.answer: The high-level problem that I’m most interested in is what I would call skill acquisition, and I’m using the term skill as some kind of sensorimotor behavior. Let me explain that with examples. The ability to walk is a skill, the ability to crawl on four legs is a skill, the ability to twirl an object in your hand is a skill, the ability to throw a ball is a skill, the ability to catch a ball is a skill, the ability to slice an apple is a skill. A skill includes a sensory aspect: the use of vision, but also touch and proprioception. All of these are important for driving the action. Then there is some physical transformation that happens; an object’s state is changed or an object is sliced or what have you. To me, that’s how I think of a central problem. We have some atomic skills, and then we combine them to produce more complex skills, and then ever more complex skills and so forth. As grown-ups, we have this wrapper with us, and therefore we can learn a fairly complex task. Suppose you are hired by a company to become a washing machine repair person. You’ll have to learn some specifics, but you start with a set of basic skills which all humans have. Another example might be driving: as a teenager, at 16, you learn to drive in 10, 15, 20 hours of driving, but that conceals a lot of stuff because it builds on skills that you acquired between zero to 16. That’s the high-level thing. That’s my research agenda: how to acquire skills, and then the meta-problem, where I want to acquire specific skills for robots and have a methodology such that the next skill I acquire I can do more quickly and efficiently.

items.question: Why did you choose walking as the first skill for your robotics research?
items.object: Robot walking as a learning problem with sensing integrated from the beginning
items.answer: In our group, the one we picked first was walking, and there’s a reason for that. First of all, walking is something which everyone can do. Walking on two legs and walking on four legs are both interesting problems. It’s common in biology because it’s connected to movement, and movement is important. It’s a problem which has been studied in robotics for decades. Boston Dynamics’ videos are seen by millions of people, but they approached the problem in a more classical control design sort of way. The challenge here was how do we approach it in a learning framework, paying a lot of attention to sensory inputs? When we got into this problem, those were the two angles that we were bringing in, which are not standard issue. I thought there has to be a developmental story for human babies, so there has to be a learning story which should work for robotics. As a person who has spent most of his career in vision, I feel that sensing has to be there from the get-go. Don’t think of sensing as something which you just add later, or you do it and then get some clean state and throw it over the wall and hope that will work. It has to be part of the system design from the beginning. That’s how we got into walking.

items.question: How do you understand generalization in machine learning?
items.object: Generalization in machine learning
items.answer: In machine learning, a central concept is generalization. We made progress in computer vision when we decided that to recognize all the chairs, we were not going to be able to write down a mathematical definition of a chair, but we would have examples. We’d give lots of example images, and then the system would learn what’s the concept of a chair. That’s generalization.

We’d give lots of example images, and then somehow the concept—we’d give lots of example images and then the system would learn what’s the concept of a chair. That’s generalization.

items.question: How do you think about rapid motor adaptation as a way of enabling robots to walk over changing terrain?
items.object: Rapid motor adaptation (RMA)
items.answer:
For me, for any motor activity, when you are walking what you need to do is walk on flat ground, stairs, inside, and in very slushy mud just after the rains, or the hiking trail, et cetera. We are able to do that. If we had exactly a fixed program, it would not work so well. You want to adapt to the terrain, hence the term adaptation. This idea connects to something that people in classical control have known about from the 50s and 60s: a field called adaptive control. But it was either in a slightly different framework, where by and large the models were linear and assumed to be known, and so on. What we are doing in the learning paradigm is something akin to that goal, but with much more modern and flexible tools, which deep learning provides.

Why rapid? The terrain can change very quickly from under our feet. If we walk and there’s something slippery in front of you, then you will start to slip, but we recover. The timescales are on the order of a second, because in walking a gait cycle is on the order of a second. If you take a misstep, you stumble and recover; that should take on that order as well. If it takes 10 seconds, it’s no good; you’ll have fallen down and could hurt yourself badly. Sadly, this happens. Old people falling is a major health crisis, really. That’s why our goal was rapid motor adaptation: adaptation on the scale of a second or less, which enables you to recover without severe falls or damage.

It’s really about changing how you are walking. Walking here means the commands you issue to the motors of the different joints in the different legs, in a way that adapts to the terrain: sand, hard ground, slush. What we developed was a technique for very rapidly inferring some aspects of the terrain and changing our behavior accordingly. This is what we call rapid motor adaptation, or RMA. It’s based on a very simple idea: if I issue the same commands to my body, how it actually reacts will depend on the terrain. If I’m walking on hard ground—let’s say I’m blind, not looking, not thinking, the absent-minded professor, just walking on hard ground—and then I walk onto the beach and now I’m in sand, what will happen? I will put my foot down and lift it up with the same force I was doing a few seconds ago. But in the sand my foot sinks, so when I lift it up, with the same force it won’t come up to the same extent. This is sensed by my proprioceptive system and tells me something is different here. How my body reacts: we have a certain desired effect, issue a command, but what actually happens is different depending on the terrain you are on. This discrepancy is the signal that we can use to adapt. I think the intuition is basically what I explained, and then there are a few technical details, but I think I’ve given you 80% of the idea right here.

items.question: How do you understand the advantage of learning-based robot control over the classical approach of writing down equations and designing a control law?
items.object: Learning-based robot control versus classical control theory
items.answer: I’ll make a little historical remark here. If you look at the history of physics over time, in the 19th century there were no computers. What clever physicists had to do to understand a phenomenon was essentially write down differential equations. Newton, Maxwell—I mean, the nature of physics was captured by these differential equations, which described the phenomena. That’s the mindset which came into control theory: you have a physical system, so you describe dynamics by some differential equations. The practical issues are that these differential equations might require knowing something about the mass, the friction, and so forth. The physics is correct, but the physics has all these unknown parameters, and these unknown parameters will keep changing as I’m walking on stairs, leaves, mud, sand. These parameters keep changing. Even though in theory the physicists have a way of understanding this, going back a couple hundred years, the practical implementation is stuck with the issue that I don’t know all these parameters. Then there is the complexity of contact. When you have legs, some legs are on the ground, some legs above the ground, and every one of these regimes requires a different model. All of this, when you try to do it in an analytical style—the old style, where you write down the equations, design a controller, do it with pen and paper, and then implement it on the computer—works well for simple systems which are identified, where we know these parameters. This is responsible for the successes of classical control. Man went into the Moon; the Apollo mission—you need to make sure the orbits around the Moon were accurate, and these kinds of capabilities were provided by techniques derived from classical control theory. In our current setup, what we have is this very complex system for which the model may not be written out in advance. Learning approaches have the benefit that they can deal with these unknowns as part of the learning process. We are identifying the system at the same time as learning a control law, and this is very powerful.

items.question: Why do you place so much confidence in computer simulation as a method for science and control engineering?
items.object: Computer simulation as a scientific and engineering method
items.answer: To return to my analogy of physics, classical physicists of the 19th century operated in a certain way, but what do physicists of the 20th century do, or post-1960 or 1952? We have access to a computer, so you don’t have to rely on an analytic solution to a differential equation. You can simulate the system, and simulate it very accurately without having to make simplifying approximations. In statistics, same thing: an earlier generation of statisticians had to make these simplifying assumptions, that n goes to infinity, there’s some distribution which is Gaussian, because that enabled you to make the math go through. If you take samples with a computer, we don’t have to make those approximations. In my view, the power of the computer and simulation is that we no longer have to make the kind of simplifying assumptions which were needed to make the math go through for previous generations of physicists, statisticians, and control engineers. Simulation is the answer in that sense. Simulation relies on having that underlying physical model, because there’s no black magic here. But simulation benefits from Moore’s Law: every year the computers get faster, the technology for simulation gets a bit more accurate. If you are relying on simulation, you’re riding that curve, whereas when I’m relying on being very clever in my head, I’m relying on human ingenuity, which doesn’t change that rapidly.

items.question: How do you think robot simulators can overcome their limited diversity compared with the real world?
items.object: Simulation diversity and the development of robot simulators
items.answer: That’s a valid point, but I view this as a matter of time. To me, the ideal simulator is not a one-shot process. I think it’s a feedback loop. When we build a simulation, we are building essentially a model of the external world. Then we train a system in that, put it out into the real world, and something doesn’t go right. That might tell us something to change in our simulation. This is itself a cycle, which I think of as more or less the scientific process, because in a way I think of a simulator as a theory and the real world as an experiment. Science is about theory and experiment, but it’s never one way; it’s a loop. That diversity you are seeking will emerge as we put more effort into this. In certain settings we can do this by capturing reality. Some of my work, a little bit at Berkeley and a little bit with colleagues at Meta, has been about simulation environments. We had one called Gibson, another called Habitat, where we scanned real-world apartments, put them inside the computer, and used them to study navigation strategies for mobile robots. It turns out that way you get the statistics of the real world in some way. Simulation rests on a variety of technologies, all of which are getting better, in my view. Think of Hollywood movies: they have very good graphics and very good physical effects. That surely tells us that’s good enough to fool us visually, so it tells us the prospects of this area are good.

items.question: How do you understand the role of vision in helping a robot navigate difficult terrain?

items.question: How do you assess the remaining challenges in robot locomotion on four legs versus two?

items.question: How do you assess progress on the core problems of computer vision?
items.object: Progress on the core problems of computer vision
items.answer: There are what I would call the classic problems of core vision. I had a slogan for this. I used to call them the three R’s of vision. One R is recognition: you have an image and you have to say, does this have a chair or a dog or a cat? I had reconstruction, which meant going to 3D, recovering a 3D shape of an object or the spatial layout of the scene. The third R, in order to make it three R’s, I called reorganization, but some people would call it segmentation or grouping, which is taking the collection of pixels and breaking them up into individual objects, for example these pixels belong to a chair, these pixels belong to a human, and so on. On these problems, we have seen remarkable progress. Recognition: I think there’s a lot of work which came out of Meta, my colleagues at Meta, and preceding work over the decades that I don’t have the time to get into. Building computer programs for recognizing cats, dogs, and chairs, we can really do remarkably well. We can do this with thousands of categories. The work in this area is really about scaling up. We can do quite well, and if you give me more data and more examples, more labels or examples, I can make it work. The practical settings remain. For example, somebody who works in medical image analysis wants to diagnose some problem in someone’s X-ray. We can use this methodology and train a system with more examples. In terms of breaking up the image into objects, that’s again a problem I’ve worked on for many years. Recently, for example, you have a system which came out of an attack on Segment Anything. It was trained on millions or even a billion examples, and with that problem can be solved. The problem of 3D reconstruction is somewhat solved, but not fully solved. The versions for which there are very good solutions are if you have multiple views of one object. This used to be called structure from motion or SLAM, and now the preferred technology is something called NeRF, neural radiance fields, and that gives remarkable pictures. But I don’t think the problem is solved at the level of what humans can do, which is that even from a single image we can solve it. I regard the problem of recovering 3D from a single image as still having large parts that are not solved.

items.question: Where do you see the important open directions connecting computer vision to other fields?
items.object: Computer vision’s connections to robotics and cognition
items.answer: Core vision doesn’t exist for its own sake, right? Vision exists for something. I think vision connects into two neighboring fields. One is robotics, vision for guiding action, and this is what I have chosen to pursue in the last five years. The other field to which vision connects is vision to cognition, and I would include language as a proxy: models which deal with vision and language together. This area is very open. I think there has been substantial progress, but a lot more to do. Vision has seen tremendous strides, but I don’t think of it as solved. There are areas like the interaction between vision and language, long-form language-video understanding: I watch a movie and want to understand it, answer questions about the movie, and that will be a combination of language and visual reasoning, obviously the applications to robotics.

items.question: What do adversarial examples in image classification tell you about how humans interpret images?
items.object: Adversarial examples in image classification
items.answer: Adding some imperceptible noise, if you will, but then you feed it to your computer program, your classifier, and it says this is a snake or something like that. It’s kind of remarkable, and we can explain these fairly easily, because what’s happening is that in these neural networks they are classifiers, so they have a decision boundary. That imperceptible noise is modifying the image in a certain direction such that it fools the classifier; it just goes over the other side of the decision boundary. But humans are not fooled by that. A human looking at that image is not fooled by that, and that tells me that the human process of interpreting an image is more sophisticated than that simple classifier. That’s a worthwhile topic for us to study.

items.question: How do you think combining top-down and bottom-up image understanding could help solve adversarial examples?
items.object: Combining top-down and bottom-up image understanding
items.answer: I have not worked on this problem myself, but I’m going to give a few throwaway remarks here. I feel that the right way to understand any image has both a bottom-up and a top-down component. The top-down component is what we exercise when we dream. items.question: How did you come to see human annotations and dataset benchmarks as a scientific foundation for computer vision?
items.object: Human annotations and dataset benchmarks as a scientific foundation for computer vision
items.answer:
This takes me back to about 2000 or something like that, or even earlier. I had a little debate at a panel with one of my colleagues called Olivier Faugeras, who was one of the people who studied the geometry of computer vision. He regarded structure from motion, SLAM, as worthwhile, respectable problems because they have a clean mathematical formulation. But he regarded problems like segmentation and recognition as kind of dubious quality, shall we say. In particular, he said segmentation: everybody writes up, submits a paper, and then they’ll have some images and say these are the groups that my system found, and then we have to accept it and be happy. This is not a way of doing science. He was very much in the French tradition where you need to have mathematical formalisms and so on.

I came back from that trip and was determined to prove him wrong. The way to think about it was: how do other sciences which have no precise mathematical models do this? Psychology and so on do experiments with humans, so the natural thing here was to think about experiments with humans. items.question: What kind of evidence did you need to be convinced that deep learning worked?
items.object: Natural-image benchmarks as evidence for deep learning
items.answer: Jeff Hinton called me, and his first question was, “Why don’t you like deep learning?” He was very direct, so I thought I needed to be direct back. I said, “Oh, because you haven’t ruled the point; you haven’t made the case.” He said, “Oh, but we have these results on MNIST and CIFAR and this.” I said those are little baby datasets, and I’m not going to be convinced by that. We need something with the complexity of natural images. I said, “For example, we have this Pascal challenge for object detection, and if you get good results on that, that would be impressive.” He hung up and called me back the next day. He said, “Pascal, I know you guys like Pascal, but I don’t think it has enough images for the techniques that we have. On the other hand, ImageNet, which also has come in, has a lot more images, and I feel that’s more promising. What do you think of that?” I said, “Yeah, I’d be impressed by ImageNet results.” He said, “Okay, I’m going to go back and I’ll make a couple of students work on this problem, and if we have something to show, I’ll call you.” Well, as they say, the rest is history. That was Alex Krizhevsky.

items.question: Why do you see medicine and healthcare as particularly promising applications of AI?
items.object: AI in medicine and healthcare
items.answer: Medicine, healthcare: these are very important. There are many, and these will not be completely transferred to AI, but the use of a human and a machine together—for example, in diagnosing X-ray images. I’m picking an example closest to my own competence. I’ve worked on things like that before, and these can be remarkable and democratizing. Think of some blood sample: taking a photo is easy now. Cameras are ubiquitous. Everybody, even in a less-developed or poor country, has access to phones and cameras. Can you use them in some ways? There was a project I knew about in India where, in underserved hospitals, you take a photo of a kid who’s just been born, and from that you can estimate aspects of whether the child was stunted in growth. Equally in America, where 18% of our GDP goes to health, that’s a big area.

items.question: Why are you personally unworried about AI taking jobs?
items.object: AI's effects on jobs and human work
items.answer: I want to say one thing because whenever there’s a discussion of AI, there’s a discussion of AI taking jobs, and I’m not worried about that personally. The reason is that we have seen the effect of computerization over time, but it takes a lot of time for systems to adapt. When the process is gradual, it goes through a process where initially you have humans and machines working together, then the machine is just assisting the human, then the human and machine work together, then some part of the work is completely outsourced to the machine. The human then starts to do something more creative and fun. If you think about programming, once upon a time people had to program in assembly language and machine instruction. I programmed a machine in the 1970s by pushing certain buttons to load the program, to bootstrap the program. Then we get to higher-level languages, and even more so. Now we use GPT to help us get a lot of the standard verbiage of the code ready. When was there ever this mass unemployment from programming? I don’t think we have seen that. What productivity has made is that we could apply these techniques across many more settings. It would not have been worthwhile to do it in the 1950s, given the effort of programming. There were many applications you would simply not have tried to computerize. I’m not a professional economist, but as an AI researcher I have to think about the consequences of my work. I tend to think it will all be in conjunction with humans, and it’s not something to worry about in that same way.

items.question: Why do you value the T model of skills for someone beginning an AI research career?
items.object: The T model of skills for AI researchers
items.answer: I always believe that people need to have a portfolio of skills. There’s something where they should be broad and some ways in which they should be narrow, like a T. Sometimes people call it the T model. I think there are some technical skills you need to master. If you train a PyTorch model or TensorFlow model, you need to understand the basic math of machine learning, basic coding abilities, and so on. There are basic core technical skills that are essential. But then there is a certain breadth of knowledge which I also appreciate, and I always tell my students to try to think outside the box. If you are doing computer vision, maybe also read the literature in perception, neuroscience, talk to people in computer graphics, even art. Our field connects to so many other disciplines. AI broadly does, and I think people who are more broad-minded can contribute more over the long scale of time.

items.question: How did you come to question the logic-based approach to artificial intelligence you worked on with John McCarthy?
items.object: John McCarthy’s logic-based approach to artificial intelligence
items.answer: I read the literature of classical AI, which was very much centered at Stanford, logic-based AI. John McCarthy was the god of that, because he had coined the term artificial intelligence. His view was that we were going to solve the intelligence problem by representing facts about the world using first-order logic and then doing logical inference. You could convert planning to be an inference problem, deducing new facts about the world as an inference problem, and so on. That’s what he believed. There was a little niggling problem at that time, which John McCarthy recognized: in common-sense reasoning, you have this problem that you give new facts and then your belief in old facts changes. The classic example is Tweety: somebody says yes, it can fly, but then somebody tells you Tweety is a penguin, so you say, oh, maybe it can’t fly. Then somebody tells you Tweety is a mechanical penguin with a motor and wings, then maybe it can fly, but then somebody tells you the motor has broken down, and so on. Humans have this ability in common-sense reasoning to change our assumptions. This is not a problem for probabilistic reasoning; with Bayesian reasoning, with every new evidence you change your beliefs. But in classical logic this is a problem. McCarthy wanted a solution to this problem in classical logic, and this was the problem he assigned me to work on. It’s a very hard problem, and nobody—I haven’t solved it. After a few years I was just getting very frustrated. Then I met Rod Brooks. He was a roboticist and a student at Stanford, and he told me over a beer that all this logic stuff is nonsense. What you really should work on is vision or robotics. He told me about Moravec’s paradox at 1 or 2 a.m. at the spot near Stanford, and it really shook me because I believed the important stuff was all this logic and reasoning.

items.question: How do you see the respective roles of small science and big science in AI research?
items.object: Small science and big science in AI research
items.answer:
I spent some time at Google and then at Meta, at that time called Facebook, Facebook AI Research, FAIR. There are different modes of industrial research. There’s a mode which is just like academia: individual investigators, maybe two or three people working together. They have an idea, implement something, do experiments, write a paper. But then you also have the possibility of these bigger teams. This is a mode which, for example, DeepMind has had and OpenAI has had, where you have a large team of people who work toward one project and you put a lot of wood behind that arrow and have a critical mass, and now you can build something much bigger. In my view both modes are important. I like to think of it as small science and big science.

There’s an analogy to physics. Some people may have seen the movie Oppenheimer. A prominent character is Ernest Lawrence, a physics professor at Berkeley. He built a cyclotron and started this tradition of big science. Before that, if you look at physics papers before 1930, you never have papers with multiple authors, maybe one, maybe two. Today you have papers in high-energy physics with a thousand authors. It started with Lawrence at Berkeley, because to build this equipment and accelerate particles fast enough led to discoveries, but people had to get together. They could no longer hope to work one person by themselves.

I think the same is true for our field. We need to acknowledge that our field has both an AI small-science component and a big-science component, and both need to be perceived. It’s not either or. Small science can do exploration a bit more readily; big science can do exploitation more readily. If you look at physics, when they do work on the Large Hadron Collider it’s all academic research, but it is big science, a bunch of universities created by a consortium. That’s my belief: it’s complementary, and I value both small science and big science.

items.question: How does reading history shape your approach to AI research?
items.object: History as a guide to AI research
items.answer: I like reading history a lot. I find history a lot of fun, and I like scientific history as well. Let me give an argument for that and why I try to encourage students to read history. There are many aspects of life where you never have exactly the same situation repeat. History is that, but you can find nearest neighbors. If you are in a situation, you can think, okay, here was a similar situation faced at this point in time. This is true in the course of human history, when we talk about kingdoms, empires, wars, revolutions, and also in the history of science. Sometimes we look at a field like physics and think of it as so beautiful and mature, but physics wasn’t like that 300 years ago, and biology wasn’t like that 50 or 100 years ago. Things were very uncertain, and there were debates and absolutely wrong ideas. When I look at that, it gives me some inspiration and confidence about AI. Today AI is on everybody’s tongue; we see it in the newspapers. When I started in the field in the 80s, it was this little discipline in a computer science department, because mostly they thought this was just talk and was never going to be real. How do you have the confidence to persist in a field when it’s really not able to deliver yet? I think by historical analogy: these other fields were also very embryonic and didn’t work. When I try to project the future of AI, I do the same. Sometimes we worry about—or extrapolate very quickly. We think suddenly this will happen.
